en: From the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Ten Evil Deeds": "Good son,
it is as if a king governs the affairs of state and possesses in abundance various precious gems such as *maṇi*,
*musāragalva*, *aśmagarbha*, *pravāda*, and *gomedaka*, as well as rare jewels and necklaces."
Riding upon death, one enters hell.

For example, it is as if an ordinary person in this world possesses in abundance horses, oxen, sheep, silk, cloth, and bolts of fabric, as well as all varieties of large and small grains and beans; yet, despite possessing these, they die and enter hell because they have not practiced the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, [it is] suffering. The Bodhisattva Jiaye addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is truly as the Sage has taught."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what is that which is wholesome?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
If all sentient beings cultivate roots of goodness, there are two [aspects]:
first, not harming sentient beings;
second, not engaging in negligence.
Third, not drinking alcohol;
fourth, not eating meat;
fifth, constantly practicing great compassion.
"Such a person does not sever their roots of goodness.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, regarding what the Buddha has said concerning those who receive the Buddha's teachings..."
"One must not drink alcohol.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa,
"Excellent, excellent!"
Understand my meaning:
those among all sentient beings who do not drink alcohol are my true children.
Then one is no longer an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Good son,
as for those who drink alcohol:
Perhaps the ruler does not recognize his minister;
perhaps the minister does not recognize his ruler;
perhaps the father does not recognize his son.
Some sons do not recognize their fathers;
some elder brothers do not recognize their younger brothers; and some younger brothers do not recognize their elder brothers.
Sometimes the elder sister does not recognize her younger sister; sometimes the younger sister does not recognize her elder sister;
and sometimes the husband does not recognize his wife.
Sometimes the wife does not recognize her husband;
sometimes the teacher does not recognize his disciple;
and sometimes the disciple does not recognize his teacher.
Or they may fail to recognize their internal or external kinsmen. Good son,
this is a present perversion.
How much more so for the future. Good son,
all sentient beings who do not eat wine or meat—
They were able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O sons of good family."
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a woman named Kṛpāṇī who sold liquor for others;
her hairpins and comb fell into a well.
Eighty thousand arhats surrounded the well and stayed there;
they drew water and drank it,
whereupon they immediately became dazed and intoxicated, losing all consciousness of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Tathāgata expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the arhats.
Having heard the Dharma, those arhats were immediately sobered from their intoxication.
He came to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I have now cultivated the Path and attained the fruits of the four stages.
For what reason do I not recognize [you] today?"
The Tathāgata Buddha addressed the sons of good family:
"In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there is a woman named Gīṣpanthā who sells wine."
"The hairpins and comb have fallen into the well.
You are now drinking water and thus becoming dazed and intoxicated.
I shall now remove this delusion for you."
I now see that you have conceived a heart of fear.
The Kinnarī woman, having caused others to suffer, has fallen into the Hell of the Saw-Bed;
this woman’s body is being sawn into a hundred pieces.
He blew them until they were reduced to fine dust;
then, they reassembled and took on form once more,
with a body three feet tall and a complexion dark blue-black.
His head was hairless and his two ears were blocked;
he lacked both eyes and had no nostrils.
His lower lip was drooping and distorted, his hands had no ten fingers, and his feet had no two soles.
This is all due to the selling of wine;
how much more so for drinking it?
Although he had previously drunk wine, he has now confessed it.
One should give rise to deep remorse as if harboring a sense of shame and humility.
Furthermore, do not drink again.
It is like a person who has contracted a grave illness.
He then encountered a skilled physician who applied medicine to it,
and by means of that medicine he was cured.
It is the same for one who practices repentance.
They gave rise to profound remorse and vowed never to do so again,
attaining the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās:
"Whether one has received the five precepts or has received the two hundred and fifty precepts,"
If one receives the precepts of complete observance of dignified conduct,
or if one receives the full precepts,
drinking alcohol is not permitted.
Those who drink alcohol commit an offense against the Prātimokṣa.
If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī commits this, they immediately enter hell;
if an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) commits it, they commit a duṣkṛta offense.
For eighty thousand kalpas, they shall enter hell.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One, wine likewise has no life."
"For what reason does the Tathāgata admonish against alcohol as being suffering?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was Aṅgulimāla."
Intoxicated by drink, he became licentious and concealed his mother;
he murdered his father, and his mother, in turn, consorted with another man and killed him with a blade.
For this reason, I now warn against alcohol as a source of suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, I admonish all laypeople and those who have left the home life:
those who receive my precepts are not permitted to serve wine to others."
One does not go to hear music at a wine shop;
one does not listen to those who strongly urge others to drink wine;
and one does not listen to those who brew grain with yeast together with others.
The śrāvaka disciples are likewise in this regard:
the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas restrain the mind,
while the śrāvakas restrain the body.
Good son, you must not permit the serving of wine to bhikṣus; if you do so,
you shall be without arms for five hundred lifetimes.
Because he brewed grain mash together with bhikṣus,
for five hundred lifetimes his ears were deaf and his hearing was severed;
he constantly could not hear the sounds of words being spoken.
A bhikṣu who [frequents] a tavern shall be mute for five hundred lifetimes;
his mouth will be unable to speak.
One who forcibly urges a bhikṣu to drink alcohol falls into the Hell of Severed Knees,
which measures eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
It was equal in length and breadth.
Within it were five hundred strongmen who fashioned swords and severed both his knees.
It is the same for one who strongly urges a bhikṣu to drink alcohol.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what kind of offense does one who eats meat incur?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent!
All sentient beings who do not eat meat..."
This is my posthumous son;
he is no ordinary person, O virtuous man.
If all sentient beings receive the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa,
O son of good family,
even if all sentient beings were to remain for an entire kalpa, they should not be permitted to eat meat.
“World-Honored One,
into which hell do those who eat meat fall?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
Those who eat meat fall into the Avīci Hell,
which is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, equal on all sides,
and has gates in the four directions.
Outside each and every gate there is fierce fire;
it spreads east, west, south, and north, penetrating the earth.
Iron walls surround it on all sides, covered overhead by iron nets.
The ground is made of red iron;
the fire from above penetrates below,
and the fire from below penetrates above.
With iron ladles, iron hooks, iron bits, and iron tongs,
they hold fire and burn them;
they drive those who eat meat into this hell to undergo its great suffering.
He felt deep remorse and was filled with shame and humility.
Furthermore, he must not eat again;
it would be like placing a bright pearl into turbid water.
By the power of the jewel, the water immediately becomes clear;
just as when smoke and clouds are removed, the moon becomes bright and clear,
so too it is with one who can repent for the evil they have committed.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"All sentient beings who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion;
those who do not eat meat possess great merit."
"A hundred thousand million parts would not equal even one part of it.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for those who boil meat, roast meat, butcher meat, and take life, how many places of rebirth are distinguished?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Those who cook meat fall into the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons,
which is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth."
Within it there is water, and beneath it there is fire.
One holds fire to burn it, until it bubbles and boils;
then the person who cooked the flesh is driven into this hell to undergo its great suffering.
The person who roasts meat falls into the Grilled Bed Hell (Taptakaṭāha),
which is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
there is an iron bed upon it and fire beneath it.
They hold fire to burn it and force the person who roasted the meat to lie upon it;
as the flesh dries up, scorches, and rots, they undergo great suffering.
Those who butcher meat fall into the Crushing Mortar Hell.
Within it are five hundred strong men who cut the victim into ten thousand pieces,
blowing them into fine dust, only for him to suffer great agony once again.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, those who eat meat are not disciples of the Tathāgata;
they are the followers of external paths."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Those who eat meat do so without awareness, without knowledge, without hearing, and without seeing;
they may even eat the flesh of their own ministers."
In some cases, a minister eats the flesh of his sovereign;
in some cases, a son eats the flesh of his father;
and in some cases, a father eats the flesh of his son.
Or a younger brother might eat the flesh of his elder brother; or an elder brother might eat the flesh of his younger brother;
or a younger sister might eat the flesh of her elder sister.
Or a sister eats her sister’s flesh;
or a wife eats her husband’s flesh;
or a husband eats his wife’s flesh.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa,
"One who eats meat eats the flesh of one's own parents and kinsmen.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, to what hell do those who eat meat fall?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa,
"Those who eat meat fall into the Hell of Excrement and Filth."
It is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
and within it the excrement is ten thousand fathoms deep;
those who eat meat are driven into this hell to undergo its great suffering.
For five million lifetimes, there will be no end to their emergence [from suffering]. Good son,
those who eat meat are like a pack of dogs vying over bones, each greedily desiring more for themselves.
It is the same for those who eat meat,
O son of good family:
to cut meat is to cut one's own father.
One who cuts flesh is cutting the flesh of his father;
he harms and injures his mother.
It is as if, when a father dies, one must slaughter an ox or a sheep, taking up a knife to harm it.
This is none other than one's own father.
The minds of all sentient beings are thus inverted;
those who eat meat are eating the flesh of their own fathers.
Those who gnaw on bones are gnawing on their father’s bones;
those who drink meat broth are drinking their father’s blood. Good son!
If any sentient beings possess a sense of shame and remorse, they should not eat meat.
Even those who have previously eaten meat may confess their transgressions, give rise to profound repentance in their hearts,
and likewise resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we only pray that the Tathāgata will explain for us:
where does one who violates the precepts of the fast fall into hell?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Those who violate the precepts of the fast fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Therein, the bodies of these hungry ghosts are five hundred yojanas in length."
His throat is like a needle;
his head is like Mount Tai;
his hands are like dragon claws.
They eat three thousand [mouthfuls] at dawn and eight hundred at dusk;
with a single shout, thirty thousand are driven away.
Those who break their fast enter this hell and undergo its great suffering.
Furthermore, having escaped this hell, they circle Mount Tai, which is as crimson as a driving cloud.
Those who have violated their fasts lean their backs against it;
their flesh dries up, withers, and rots, as they undergo great suffering.
Furthermore, having departed from this suffering, one undergoes rebirth by changing form.
Good son, if one has finished eating the fast-food, [one may proceed].
Those who wrap up offerings for a vegetarian feast and give them to their parents, siblings, sovereigns, ministers, teachers, elders, friends,
or acquaintances will, in future lives, fall into the Iron Wheel Hell;
they will enter through the left armpit and emerge from the right side, with molten copper poured into their mouths.
It is the same for those who consume food during the observance of the fast.
The Buddha said:
"Those who eat chicken meat shall fall into hell."
The three people together shall repay [the debt], and as they welcome one another, they enter hell together.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is truly as the holy teaching says; it is truly as the holy teaching says."
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we pray that the Tathāgata will explain for us:
how much merit is obtained by one who does not drink alcohol and does not eat meat?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Suppose there were a person who used elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, lapis lazuli, precious jewels, necklaces, kingdoms, cities, wives, and children as offerings in almsgiving;
this would still not be equal to a person who is able to abstain from wine and meat."
It does not equal even one part in a hundred thousand million.
Setting that matter aside,
suppose there were someone who, with hundreds of thousands of measures of gold filling the entire trichiliocosm, were to give it all away as a gift.
Furthermore, this is still not as good as someone who can renounce even one part in a hundred thousand million of meat and wine;
let alone that matter,
suppose there were someone capable of casting gold into human forms and giving hundreds of them away in charity.
Furthermore, this is not even equal to someone who is able to abstain from alcohol and meat;
it does not approach even one part in a hundred thousand million of that merit.
Let us set this matter aside for now.
Even if someone were to create banners, flowers, and precious canopies that completely filled the trichiliocosm,
it would still not equal the merit of someone who is able to abstain from alcohol and meat.
Even a hundred thousand millionth part does not equal one [fraction] of it.
Setting that matter aside,
suppose there were someone who constructed great stūpas and jeweled towers, with eaves following one after another like rice, hemp, bamboo, or reeds, reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven.
It is not as good as someone being able to abstain from alcohol and meat;
even a hundred thousand millionth part does not equal one such person. Good son.
One who does not eat meat is a bodhisattva in the present life and is no longer an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Good son,
one who does not eat meat is always free from the perception of meat.
When those who eat meat see [living beings], they conceive thoughts of harm and immediately give rise to the perception of meat.
For this reason, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is truly as the noble ones have said... [The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"All sentient beings are like, for example, a man who is destitute, solitary, and aged, and who later gives birth to an only son whom he loves exceedingly. He takes two balls of rice and offers them both to his infant son; [the child] takes the gold and leaves the rice."
All sentient beings are likewise... [as if] giving birth, just like a compassionate father; sentient beings do not bestow upon me...
*The Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapter on the Ten Evil Deeds*.
